clue.text: District in need of replanning most of you call it

indicators.note: letters that need replanning are to be laid out afresh in a new order
most of the word you means it loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A district that needs redevelopment, which most residents simply call 'it'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' trims YOU to YO; 'in need of replanning' shuffles YO + CALL + IT into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A locality is a neighbourhood or area, the same idea as a district.

clue.text: Sail hoisted thus, seeing such rocks

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing these rocks, not a noun

indicators.note: in a down clue, hoisting raises the word so its letters read upwards

parts.note: sic is Latin for thus

explanation.surface: A sail is raised, and certain rocks come into view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hoisted' turns SAIL into LIAS, itself the name of a rock series.
explanation.definitionFit: Liassic describes rocks of the Lias, the early Jurassic strata of limestone and shale.

clue.text: Dare to use up a length of cloth in alteration

indicators.note: the cloth measure goes inside the word for alteration

parts.note: a change is an alteration

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: an ell is an old measure of cloth

explanation.surface: A tailor dares to use up a stretch of fabric on alterations.
explanation.walkthrough: An ell is an old English cloth measure of about 45 inches. 'up' reverses it, as this is a down clue; 'to use' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A challenge is a dare, a call to do something bold.

clue.text: Suffer defeat about legislation for milk product

indicators.note: the word for defeat goes round the piece of legislation

parts.note: to lose is to suffer defeat
an Act is a piece of legislation

explanation.surface: A dairy bill is beaten in Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Lactose is the sugar found in milk.

clue.text: Terrible start in opera role

indicators.note: a terrible beginning is badly made, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A singer gets off to an awful beginning in an operatic part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' rearranges the eight letters of 'start in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tristan is the hero of Wagner's opera Tristan und Isolde.

clue.text: A chirpy type but a bounder, men of intelligence hold

indicators.note: the spies are said to hold the cad, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: the CIA is the US Central Intelligence Agency, whose men work in intelligence
a bounder is an old word for a cad, a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: Something that chirps turns out to be a scoundrel guarded by secret agents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounder' suggests a leaping creature, but it is the old British slang for a cad.
explanation.definitionFit: The cicada is an insect famous for its loud chirping song.

clue.text: Associate officer placed over confederacy'

indicators.note: in a down clue, what is placed over another piece comes before it

parts.note: Col is short for colonel, an officer
a league is a confederacy or alliance

explanation.surface: An officer is given command of an alliance and an associate.
explanation.definitionFit: A colleague is a fellow worker or partner.

clue.text: This guilty party has been embarrassing the Republicans

definitions.text: This guilty party has been embarrassing the Republicans

parts.words: This guilty party has been embarrassing the Republicans
parts.note: a political scandal reading: the one responsible for shaming a party is simply the wrongdoer

explanation.surface: A political scandal in which someone has shamed the party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' suggests a political party, but the guilty party is just the offender.
explanation.definitionFit: A culprit is the person to blame for a wrongdoing.

clue.text: Comes down in the main water channels

explanation.surface: A pilot lands at sea, and there are drainage trenches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is the open sea; an aircraft that ditches lands on water in an emergency.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is an emergency landing at sea by aircraft; the other is trenches dug for drainage.

clue.text: An artist rejected style shown by a student as anti-government

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the artist's letters run backwards

parts.note: RA stands for Royal Academician, a crossword artist
chic means stylishness
L is the learner plate, a student driver

explanation.surface: An artist rejects the style a student shows, calling it subversive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns RA into AR.
explanation.definitionFit: Anarchy is the absence of government, so something anarchical opposes rule by a state.

clue.text: Used to stop the rift in Tennyson's instrument?

explanation.surface: A remedy for the crack in the poet's musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson wrote of 'the little rift within the lute'; lute is also a clay or cement for sealing joints and gaps.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a sealing paste plugging cracks; the other is the stringed instrument in the Tennyson line about a little rift.

clue.text: Tellurian sailor's a very fine fellow

parts.note: a salt is an old sailor
tellurian means belonging to our planet, terrestrial

explanation.surface: An earthbound seaman is a splendid chap.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces appear in reverse order in the clue; the 's is read as 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical phrase describes a thoroughly decent, worthy person.

clue.text: "Age shall not weary them, nor the years…" (Binyon)

definitions.text: "Age shall not weary them, nor the years…" (Binyon)

parts.words: "Age shall not weary them, nor the years…" (Binyon)
parts.note: a quotation with its final word left out: the next word in Binyon's line is the one to supply

explanation.surface: A line from the remembrance poem For the Fallen, left unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurence Binyon's poem, recited at British Remembrance Day services, runs 'Age shall not weary them, nor the years ...' and the gap is filled by its next word.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb in the poem means to sentence or pronounce doom upon.

clue.text: Rich man — the subject of Shylock's ominous dream?

definitions.text: the subject of Shylock's ominous dream?

explanation.surface: A wealthy man, and what the moneylender dreamed of as an evil omen.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Merchant of Venice Shylock says 'I did dream of money-bags tonight', taking it as a bad sign.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is slang for a wealthy person, and also the sacks of cash Shylock dreamed of.

clue.text: Boaster -who took tea noisily in the middle of Meredith's novel

indicators.note: placed in the middle of the novel's title, splitting it into two equal halves

parts.note: The Egoist is a novel by George Meredith

indicators.note: said out loud, the drink sounds just like a single letter

parts.note: the drink tea sounds like the letter T

explanation.surface: A braggart slurps his tea halfway through reading a Victorian novel.
explanation.walkthrough: George Meredith's 1879 novel is The Egoist; the letter T goes in its centre.
explanation.definitionFit: An egotist talks constantly of himself, as a braggart does.

clue.text: Involve in charge in horse-race under one mile

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece under another comes after it

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
the single letter M is the usual abbreviation for a mile in distances

indicators.note: the abbreviation for in charge goes inside the race

parts.note: a plate is a horse race for a prize
IC is military shorthand for the officer in charge, as in 2IC for second in command

explanation.surface: A jockey is drawn into a charge during a race below one mile.
explanation.walkthrough: A plate is a horse race run for a prize trophy; 'under' places the race piece below one and mile in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To implicate someone is to show them to be involved in a crime.

clue.text: In retrospect some phenomenal bloomer

indicators.note: looking back means reading the letters from right to left
only some of the word phenomenal is used, a run of its letters

explanation.surface: Looking back, a phenomenal blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' takes ENOMENA from inside 'phenomenal' and 'In retrospect' reads it backwards. 'Bloomer' looks like a mistake but means a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: An anemone is a flowering plant, and a flower is something that blooms.

clue.text: Turn out on the river for training

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another sits above it
turn letters out of their places, so the word is rearranged

parts.note: the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A rowing crew turns out on the river for practice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' turns TURN into NURT; the URE is a Yorkshire river and a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Nurture means upbringing or rearing, a kind of training.

clue.text: Like the dance of Saint- Saens with Widdicombe transport, carriage included

definitions.text: Like the dance of Saint- Saens

indicators.note: the carriage is included inside the mare

parts.note: in the folk song Widdicombe Fair, Uncle Tom Cobley and all ride Tom Pearse's old grey mare
a cab is a carriage

explanation.surface: A Saint-Saens dance with a horse from a folk song pulling a carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: Saint-Saens wrote Danse Macabre. Widdicombe Fair is an English folk song about a borrowed grey mare.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint-Saens's tone poem is the Danse Macabre, a gruesome dance of death.

clue.text: Ten-footer's retrograde step in unusually odd circumstances

indicators.note: the backward step goes inside the rearranged letters
set out in an unusual way, so the letters of odd are rearranged
moving backwards, so the step's letters are read in reverse

parts.note: a pace is a step

explanation.surface: A ten-footed creature backs away in strange circumstances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retrograde' reverses the step and 'unusually' rearranges ODD into D-OD so it can surround it; 'circumstances' merely rounds off the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Decapods are crustaceans such as crabs and lobsters with ten legs.

clue.text: Gallic style sop to Cerberus

explanation.surface: A French manner, and a bribe for the guard dog of the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: A sop to Cerberus is a bribe to silence a guard; the French word also means sweetness or gentleness.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrowed from French for sweetness of manner, the word also means a tip or bribe.

clue.text: It's about the advertisement for a ship's beam

parts.note: ca is short for circa, about
taken as written

explanation.surface: A poster about a timber on a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathead is a beam projecting from a ship's bow for hoisting the anchor.

clue.text: A drop of French perfume

parts.note: de is French for of
a scent is a perfume

explanation.surface: Just a drop of French fragrance.
explanation.definitionFit: A descent is a downward slope or fall.

clue.text: But there's nothing unstable about these orographical features

definitions.text: But there's nothing unstable about these orographical features

parts.words: But there's nothing unstable about these orographical features
parts.note: the joke plays on a word meaning shaky, used in the name of a great mountain chain that is anything but

explanation.surface: Some mountains are perfectly solid, whatever their name says.
explanation.walkthrough: Orographical means relating to mountains; 'rocky' can mean wobbly or unsteady.
explanation.definitionFit: The North American range is a set of mountains, and mountains are orographical features.

clue.text: Not sounding like some bells

explanation.surface: Silent, as certain bells are.
explanation.walkthrough: Dumb-bells are weights for exercise, not bells that ring at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumb means making no sound, and dumb-bells are gym weights.

clue.text: Declare Eeyore's appetite to be insatiable?

parts.note: Eeyore is the donkey in Winnie-the-Pooh, so an ass
an appetite never satisfied is one that always ate, forever eating

explanation.surface: Proclaim that the gloomy donkey can never be filled up.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a whimsical reading: an insatiable donkey is an ass who ever ate.
explanation.definitionFit: To asseverate is to state solemnly or affirm, a formal way to declare.

clue.text: No OK to define in a word this parliamentary closure

definitions.text: No OK to define in a word

explanation.surface: A one-word definition for a nook, and the break when Parliament stops sitting.
explanation.walkthrough: Close up 'No OK' and it becomes NOOK; a one-word definition of that is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A nook is an alcove or niche; Parliament's holiday break is also called by this word.

clue.text: U.s. General is about to pass on the slope

indicators.note: the general goes round the other piece, so it is placed inside

parts.note: Ulysses S. Grant was a US Civil War general
to pass on is to die

explanation.surface: An American general is about to die on the hillside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'U.S. General' tempts towards GI, but here it is Ulysses S. Grant, who led the Union armies in the American Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: A gradient is the steepness or incline of a hill.
